rows.description: A child whose parents respond only to marks feels loved for performance and hides mistakes; the harm is less the standard than the sense that love depends on meeting it.
A teenager is praised for flawless work and neat notebooks, and learns that love and safety come with being perfect. The standard feels like a strength at first, and hides the fear underneath.

rows.subtype: Friend all good then all bad [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager describes a friend as perfect one week and as a total traitor the next after a small slight; strong feelings make it hard to hold both good and disappointing sides together.
A child offers, "I do the cars, you do the books, then we read a story." Splitting the work and naming the reward gets it moving.

rows.subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]
rows.description: A child declares boredom after ten minutes and wants a screen; boredom is uncomfortable but can also be the doorway to imagination when adults give time and simple materials.
Left without screens on a long summer afternoon, a child builds a fort, invents a game or draws for hours. Tolerated boredom is where self-directed interest first grows.
A child who stumbles while reading makes a silly face and gets the class laughing with them; the joke keeps control of the moment, though constant clowning can hide worry.
A child giggles at funny faces, wrong words and sudden surprises. Early humour is about incongruity and safety, and laughing together bonds a child to a caregiver.
A child says a project will be quick and starts the night before. He imagines the ideal path and forgets past delays.

rows.subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
rows.description: A child says the drawing will take five minutes and is surprised when an hour has gone. Children have little felt sense of duration, so promises of soon or quickly are sincere but unreliable.
A teenager delays a project because a poor result would reveal weakness; putting it off protects the self-image but makes the eventual work worse.

With the deadline near, fear finally gives energy and the assignment is done overnight. It often works well enough to teach the wrong lesson that delaying is fine, while the cost of stress and quality is ignored.
